title: Four more ways in which teachers can help or hinder learning - 2
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton continues his portrait of learning-focused teachers, building on the earlier image of teachers as roadies rather than stars. He says such teachers know what learning is and looks like, comparing classrooms without that knowledge to Bake Off contestants working blind, and he notes that teacher training often never covered learning. They create the right context for knowledge, skills and understanding rather than one lesson format, reward small gains and treat poor behaviour as another thing to learn. They ask seven standing questions about learning and back every answer with evidence. He argues that classrooms must stop being private spaces, and that teachers should test new ideas rather than rush at them.
points: Many classrooms resemble the Bake Off segment because teachers were never taught what learning's ingredients or finished form look like.
Learning-focused teachers vary lesson design for knowledge, skills and understanding and reward approximately-right work.
They answer a set of questions about learning with real evidence, such as who is treading water, drowning or moving from Beginning to Developing.
Treating the classroom as a private space blocks improvement; teachers need colleagues in the room to see what they cannot.
quotes: Seeing ourselves as roadies gives teachers a chance to see where our real contribution takes place. The classroom is not our stage; that belongs, with our support, to the learners.

In schools, more classrooms are like this Bake Off segment than we would like to admit. In these classrooms, not enough people know what the ingredients are that make up learning or what they look like.
At one level, it isn’t the teachers’ fault. Teachers in their hundreds have told me that their college experience didn’t cover learning.

Learning-focused teachers don’t see poor behaviour as a deficit model experience. Along with some of their colleagues, they see inappropriate behaviour as an opportunity to get better; they see it as another kind of learning.

There is a danger in answering the seven questions we have listed above; it is possible to answer them glibly with very quick ‘Yes’ or No’ responses. So it is important to remember that these sentences are designed not to produce simple quick responses but to help identify the evidence about learning that enables us to answer the questions. What makes them rigorous is not each question but the quality of evidence that supports the response we make to each question.

That perception of the classroom as private space is one of the things that really has to change. It’s amazing - deep breath; in my view, a disgrace - that a profession supposedly interested in helping young people get better is so resistant to enabling its own workforce to get better.

They are slower to adopt new ideas, slower to grab at the next new thing and slower to immediately accept practices that appear to be useful until they have tested them out and found them to be true in their context. For learning-focused teachers, their demand for evidence before action applies to everything new as well as everything old.
